# The Map {#sec-map .unnumbered}

Optimization methods are easiest to understand by what they need to know about a
problem and what they promise in return. This page lays out the book along those two
lines.

## What a method needs to know

The first question to ask of any problem is what can be computed about the objective
at a point, and what structure the problem has.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-map
%%| fig-cap: "Choosing a family of methods by the structure of the problem."
flowchart TD
    Q{"What do you know<br/>about the objective?"}
    Q -->|"linear objective,<br/>linear constraints"| LP["Linear programming"]
    Q -->|"sum of squares"| LS["Least squares,<br/>regularization"]
    Q -->|"smooth, with<br/>gradients"| C{"Constraints?"}
    C -->|"none"| G["Gradient and curvature<br/>methods"]
    C -->|"equalities,<br/>inequalities"| K["KKT, barrier,<br/>ADMM"]
    Q -->|"smooth part +<br/>simple kink"| P["Proximal gradient"]
    Q -->|"values only,<br/>or many local minima"| D["Derivative-free and<br/>global search"]
    Q -->|"a likelihood<br/>built from data"| E["Estimation"]
```

The boxes correspond to chapters: linear programming to @sec-linear-programming; least
squares and proximal gradient to @sec-least-squares; gradient and curvature methods to
@sec-gradient-methods; KKT conditions, the barrier method and ADMM to
@sec-constraints; derivative-free and global search to @sec-derivative-free; and
estimation to @sec-estimation.

## What a method promises

Structure buys guarantees. The more a problem has, the stronger the promise:

| problem | typical method | what it promises |
|---|---|---|
| linear program | simplex, interior point | the exact optimum, or a proof there is none |
| convex, smooth | gradient methods, Newton | the global minimum, at a known rate set by the condition number |
| convex, constrained | barrier method, ADMM | the global minimum, with a duality gap that certifies how close |
| smooth, non-convex | the same gradient methods | a stationary point, usually a local minimum |
| black box, multimodal | annealing, populations, Bayesian optimization | a good point within the budget; no certificate |

: Guarantees by problem class. {#tbl-guarantees}

The first two parts of the book live in the top rows, where answers are exact or
certified. Part III moves down the table, where methods keep working but promise less,
and asks the question that makes modern machine learning possible at all: why local
methods find good answers on enormous non-convex problems (@sec-high-dim).

## The thread through the chapters

Four ideas recur, and following them is a good way to read the book.

- **Slope and curvature** (@sec-geometry) drive every gradient method
  (@sec-gradient-methods) and reappear as the uncertainty of an estimate
  (@sec-estimation) and the spectrum of a neural network's loss (@sec-high-dim).
- **The condition number** sets the speed of gradient descent, the accuracy of least
  squares (@sec-least-squares), and the reason regularization helps.
- **Multipliers** turn constraints into prices (@sec-constraints), from the shadow prices
  of a linear program (@sec-linear-programming) to the link prices of a fair network
  (@sec-applications).
- **Local versus global**: convexity makes local answers global; without it, methods
  either accept a local answer or spend their budget exploring (@sec-derivative-free).

## Reading paths

- **The full course**: Chapters 1 to 9 in order.
- **Machine learning**: @sec-geometry, @sec-gradient-methods, @sec-least-squares,
  @sec-estimation, @sec-high-dim.
- **Operations research and engineering**: @sec-geometry, @sec-linear-programming,
  @sec-constraints, @sec-derivative-free, @sec-applications.
- **Choosing a method for a problem at hand**: this page, then
  [Choosing an Algorithm](../appendix-choosing-an-algorithm.qmd).
